A healthy Spider plant produces baby plantlets on long stems, and these can be rooted in water or soil to grow new plants. The Spider plant tolerates moderate to low light, though variegation fades and new plantlets form more slowly in dim conditions. Brown leaf tips are the most common complaint with the Spider plant and usually trace to fluoride, chlorine, or salt buildup in the soil.

La Cinta tolera luz moderada a baja, aunque la variegación se desvanece y los hijuelos se forman más despacio en condiciones oscuras. Una Cinta sana produce hijuelos en tallos largos, y estos pueden enraizarse en agua o en sustrato para obtener nuevas plantas.

A pot with drainage holes is important for the Rubber plant because the roots will rot in soil that stays saturated. The Rubber plant is typically repotted every two to three years, or when roots begin circling the pot or emerging from the drainage holes. When repotting the Rubber plant, choose a container only one size larger to avoid leaving excess wet soil around the roots.

Una maceta con orificios de drenaje es importante para el árbol del caucho, porque las raíces se pudren en tierra que permanece encharcada. El árbol del caucho suele trasplantarse cada dos o tres años, o cuando las raíces empiezan a girar dentro de la maceta o asoman por los orificios de drenaje. Al trasplantar el árbol del caucho, elija un recipiente solo una talla más grande para evitar dejar exceso de tierra húmeda alrededor de las raíces.

cases.observed: Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) grows best in bright, indirect light and keeps its variegation strongest under those conditions. A Pothos will survive in low light, but its leaves turn more solidly green and the stems grow leggy with wider gaps between leaves. Leggy, sparse growth on a Pothos points to insufficient light, and moving it to a brighter spot encourages fuller foliage.

cases.observed: Water the Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) when the top 2 to 3 centimeters of soil have dried out, which is often about once every 7 to 10 days in active growth. In winter the Monstera needs less frequent watering, often only once every 2 to 3 weeks, because growth slows and the soil stays moist longer. Yellowing leaves on a Monstera (Monstera deliciosa) most commonly point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry further before the next watering.
